name: Wendy Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashby Lane Farm, which has six hundred sows indoors and about two hundred and fifty hectares of barley and wheat that mostly go to feed them. I'm in the farrowing house, where the sows give birth and feed the piglets for their first four weeks. My day starts at six with checking every pen, counting piglets, spotting any that are weak, and then it's feeding, cleaning and a lot of paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You came to pigs from somewhere else?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was office manager at a builders' merchant for twenty-two years, ordering, invoices, staff rotas. A big chain bought it and moved all the office work to their head office, so at fifty-four I was out. My neighbour Kevin owns Ashby Lane and said he needed someone who wasn't scared of mess or numbers, and I said I'd try the mess.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a sow settles and the piglets line up to feed, all twelve in a row, it's ridiculous and lovely. What wears me out is losing piglets. Some get lain on by the mother, and I still take it harder than Kevin's head stockman, Dennis, who's done this thirty years and just writes it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I use it every day and it's brilliant. When I started, the sow records were on a whiteboard and bits of card. I asked an AI to help me build a spreadsheet, and now Kevin can see which sows are doing well at a glance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's made me more useful than I'd be otherwise. I'm still slow with the animals, but I'm quick with the numbers, and that's kept me in the job, honestly. Dennis can hear a piglet in trouble from the yard, and I can tell Kevin what the feed bill will be in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building on it. Next I want to track which boars give the best litters, which Dennis does in his head. We've got about four months saved, and Graham, my husband, and I would keep it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dennis think of the spreadsheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He calls it Wendy's telly. But last month he came into the office and asked me to look up a sow's last three litters, so he's coming round. He'd never admit it in front of Kevin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're still slow with the animals. Tell me about a moment that showed it.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a sow was farrowing and a piglet came out not breathing. Dennis grabbed it, cleared its mouth, rubbed it hard with straw and it squealed. I just stood there holding the towel.

S0.say: I'd say I use it every day and it's brilliant, because it helped me turn whiteboard sow records into a spreadsheet. Now Kevin can see which sows are doing well at a glance.
S0.think: Privately it's made me more useful, because I'm slow with the animals but quick with numbers. That's what has kept me in the job.
S0.do: Builds on the records by tracking which boars give the best litters. Keeps about four months of savings with her husband Graham.
S0.feel: Calm, and quite pleased with herself.
S0.quote: I just stood there holding the towel.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy brings her office skills into a pig shed and knows that's her real value to the farm. She's honest about her weakness with the animals and admires Dennis's instinct. The spreadsheet has quietly changed how the farm is run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is the best kind, people can adjust. Fewer beginners is a worry for farming, but honestly farms weren't hiring many anyway. I'd say it online, I'm on a pig farmers' forum, and they'd argue with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in a good spot. I'm the beginner who can use the tools, so when tasks get automated I'm the one who sets it up. If they hire fewer beginners, the ones they keep will be like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk Kevin into a few more gadgets, cameras over the farrowing pens maybe, the kind that warn you when a sow's about to give birth. I'd take a short course in pig health, because that's my weak spot. And I'd look at putting a bit more into my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of me is even looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josh, our nineteen-year-old, who does the muck and feeding. He's not interested in screens at all. If the routine jobs shrink, he's exactly the beginner who doesn't get hired next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Dennis like cameras over the pens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate them. He'd say, a sow tells you she's about to farrow by building a nest out of nothing, you don't need a camera for that. And he's right. But Dennis sleeps, and the camera doesn't.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is the best kind and farms weren't hiring many beginners anyway. I'd say it on the pig farmers' forum and they'd argue with me.
S1.think: Off the record I'm in a good spot, because I'm the beginner who can use the tools. If they hire fewer beginners, the ones they keep will be like me.
S1.do: Talks Kevin into gadgets like farrowing cameras and takes a short pig health course. Looks at putting more into her pension.
S1.quote: But Dennis sleeps, and the camera doesn't.
S1.fieldNote: She sees slow change as her opportunity and says so plainly. Her worry goes to Josh, the young worker who doesn't like screens. She respects Dennis's skill completely while still wanting the camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I got out of the office just in time, and I'd mean it as a joke, mostly. I'd say people should learn the tools instead of fighting them. Politicians shouting about it doesn't help anyone retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think about my old team at the merchant, and about my daughter Lucy. She's a paralegal, she prepares documents for solicitors, and that's exactly the routine work these assistants would take. She's twenty-nine and bright, but bright isn't always enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Lucy and show her how I use these tools, so she becomes the one in her office who runs them, not the one replaced by them. I'd keep our savings as they are, in case she needs help. And I'd tell Kevin to start letting the AI do our feed orders, saving me an hour a day for the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Lucy. For me, oddly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you got out just in time. Did it feel lucky then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at all. I cried in the car park on my last day and Graham had to drive me home. I only see it as luck now, looking back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucy if she rang you crying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I was fifty-four, standing in a car park with a box, and now I'm counting piglets and happier than I've been in years. I'd say, it's not the end, it's just a door you didn't choose. And then I'd drive over with a lasagne.

S2.say: I'd joke that I got out of the office just in time, and say people should learn the tools instead of fighting them. Politicians shouting doesn't help anyone retrain.
S2.think: Privately I'd think about my old team and my daughter Lucy, a paralegal who prepares documents for solicitors. That's exactly the routine work these assistants would take.
S2.do: Shows Lucy how she uses AI tools so Lucy becomes the one who runs them. Keeps savings ready to help and gets the farm's feed orders handled by AI to free an hour a day for the pigs.
S2.feel: Uneasy for her daughter and oddly calm for herself.
S2.quote: It's not the end, it's just a door you didn't choose.
S2.fieldNote: She has already lived through losing an office job to centralisation, and that gives her both calm and authority. The car park memory showed that her 'lucky' story was painful at the time. Her help for Lucy is very practical: tools, then lasagne.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too fast and the gains need sharing fairly, though I don't trust either side to do it well. Something like a one-off tax on the biggest winners, maybe. I'd say it on the forum and get shouted at from both directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the pigs are fine in this one. Nobody's going to replace a farrowing house with a chatbot. But the price of pork depends on people having money, and if lots of office workers lose jobs, they'll buy cheaper meat, and Kevin will feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Kevin cut costs with the AI, feed, energy, vet bills, so the farm stays ahead. I'd give Lucy whatever she needed for a few months, rent or retraining. And Graham and I would hold off on the new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The pigs are safe, but the people who buy them aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust neither side to share it well. Who would you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, people like Kevin, who run something small and know everyone's name. Not that they should run the country. But they understand that if the workers go under, the business goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did Lucy's job survive in this picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Unless she'd become the person who runs the tools, like we planned. I'd hope so, but I'm not daft.

S3.say: I'd say it's gone too fast and the gains need sharing fairly, maybe with a one-off tax on the biggest winners. I'd say it on the forum and get shouted at from both directions.
S3.think: I think the pigs are fine, but pork prices depend on people having money. If office workers lose jobs, they'll buy cheaper meat and Kevin will feel it.
S3.do: Uses AI to help Kevin cut feed, energy and vet costs so the farm stays ahead. Gives Lucy money for rent or retraining and postpones the new kitchen.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because the pigs are safe but the people who buy them aren't.
S3.quote: Nobody's going to replace a farrowing house with a chatbot.
S3.fieldNote: She thinks about the farm as a business, following the money from office jobs to pork prices. Her centre view is distrust of both sides, with trust reserved for small owners like Kevin. She's honest that Lucy's job probably wouldn't survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need rules, proper safety testing and help for workers to switch. I'm all for new technology, but not without a plan. I'd say it on the forum, and this time I think people would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I got out of the office just before the computers came for it. If robots come for the pig shed, I've run out of places to jump to. Cleaning, feeding, even the muck, all of it can be done by a machine in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kevin to make me the person who runs the robots and the cameras, because I'm already the one with the spreadsheet. I'd look at the pig health course again, the bit no machine does well, like spotting a sick sow early. And Graham and I would add another month to our savings by cutting holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the machines, frightened about my age, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josh, for sure, and probably Dennis, though Dennis would retire rather than learn it. Josh is nineteen and has never wanted anything but to feed the pigs. I'd hate to be the person who sets up the robot that takes his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd set it up anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If I don't, Kevin will pay a company to do it and then I'm out too. That's the honest answer, and I don't like how it sounds.

S4.say: I'd say this is where we need rules, safety testing and help for workers to switch. I'm all for new technology, but not without a plan.
S4.think: I got out of the office just before the computers came for it, and if robots come for the pig shed I've run out of places to jump to. Cleaning, feeding and muck can all be done by machines.
S4.do: Asks Kevin to make her the person who runs the robots and cameras and takes the pig health course on spotting sick sows early. Adds another month to savings by cutting holidays.
S4.feel: Anxious, excited about the machines and frightened about her age at once.
S4.quote: If robots come for the pig shed, I've run out of places to jump to.
S4.fieldNote: Her adaptability is her strategy, but she knows it has limits at fifty-eight. The hardest moment was admitting she'd set up the robot that takes young Josh's job. She doesn't like how it sounds and says so anyway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because I've jumped once already and I don't have another jump in me. What would help is training paid for by the companies making the robots, for the people already on the farms. And some help for lads like Josh, who are good with animals and not with screens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I like the change. I do, mostly. I just want to be one of the people it happens with, not one of the people it happens to.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: My pleasure. Come back at Christmas and I'll show you the piglets, you'll never eat bacon again. No, you will, everyone does.

headlineQuote: I got out of the office just before the computers came for it. If robots come for the pig shed, I've run out of places to jump to.
portrait: Wendy is a 58-year-old former office manager who lost her job when a chain bought her builders' merchant, and now works in the farrowing house on a pig and arable farm. She uses AI every day and has made herself useful by turning the farm's records into a spreadsheet, though she's still slow with the animals. She sits in the middle politically and trusts small owners more than either side. In the office scenarios she worries for her paralegal daughter; with robots, she'd run them herself while hating what that means for the young worker Josh.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because she has already changed careers once and doesn't think she can do it again.
whatWouldHelp: Training paid for by the companies making the robots, for people already on farms, and help for young workers who are good with animals but not screens.
